query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high-temperature salt exposures (~800 °C), the pre-formed passivation film on Q235 steel transforms into a brittle, defect-rich Fe-oxide layer that readily cracks under thermal stresses, permitting aggressive chloride ion penetration and accelerating localized pitting corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-passivated Q235 steel with a dense, dark, uniform passivation film produced by pickling and passivation treatment.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to cyclic salt spray in a controlled furnace at 800 °C versus a reference exposure at room temperature (25 °C).
generation.conditions: Aggressive salt (NaCl) environment under cyclic thermal exposure at 800 °C, compared to constant room temperature exposure; testing durations sufficient to capture film transformation (e.g., multiple cycles over 8–12 days).
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation of the initial passive film into brittle Fe2O3/Fe3O4 phases with increased microcracking and defect density upon high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation kinetics and induces thermal expansion mismatch. This, in combination with chloride attack, creates film defects and cracks, allowing chloride ions to penetrate and initiate pitting corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the room temperature reference, the high-temperature group will show significantly higher corrosion rates (e.g., weight loss increased by roughly 50%), higher pit density observed by SEM, and EDS analysis confirming altered oxide compositions.
generation.baseline: Pre-passivated Q235 steel exposed to salt spray at room temperature, where the film remains more intact and corrosion proceeds slowly.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should not apply if the ambient temperature is maintained below a threshold (e.g., <500 °C) where thermal stress is insufficient to induce film cracking.
generation.uncertainty: Variability in film homogeneity and initial defect densities; challenges in precisely controlling thermal cycling parameters at extreme temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of pre-passivated Q235 steel specimens; subject one set to cyclic salt spray at 800 °C and the other at room temperature. After exposure, perform SEM imaging, weight loss measurements, and EDS to analyze oxide compositions and pit densities.
measurements: SEM images for microcracking and pit density
EIS to assess charge transfer resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature specimens do not exhibit significantly higher weight loss, pit density, or altered oxide compositions (i.e., no statistical difference compared to room temperature specimens), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the corrosion behavior and mechanism of Q235 in atmospheric environment are studied by designing a cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion experiment. The specific conclusions are as follows: Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of the accelerated corrosion process can be roughly divided into four stages: (1) passivation film corrosion product generation and local shedding, (2) matrix rust layer generation and covering, (3) rust layer accumulation and stacking onto a flat and dense second protective layer, and (4) matrix rust layer breaking through the protective layer continues to grow thicker until shedding. After pickling passivation treatment of Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of corrosion from passivation film weakness, pitting corrosion gradually develops into comprehensive corrosion with the elongation of time. Rust layer composition gradually transitions from passivation products into iron oxide based on hydroxyl iron oxide. The whole process is “from point to surface” corrosion. In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.

papers.title: Research on the Corrosion Behavior of Q235 Pipeline Steel in an Atmospheric Environment through Experiment.
papers.system: Pre-passivated Q235 low‐carbon steel (pipeline samples) subjected to cyclic salt spray tests
papers.approach: Samples were prepared by pickling and passivation; cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion tests were performed with weight loss, macroscopic and microscopic surface analyses, and EDS to monitor the evolution of corrosion features over time.
papers.findings: The study delineated corrosion evolution in stages – initial passivation film corrosion with localized shedding, formation of a matrix rust layer, development of a secondary protective layer, and eventual breakdown of the rust covering. The passivation film initially provides a barrier via electrochemical protection, but chloride ions infiltrate and induce pitting, leading to eventual film rupture and accelerated corrosion.
papers.mechanism: The protective nature of the pre-existing passivation film eventually succumbs to chloride-induced local breakdown. Once cracked, the film permits differential aeration and pitting, causing localized rust formation that may temporarily offer secondary protection before further deterioration.

papers.title: The Effect of Temperatures on the Passivation Behavior of Q235 Steel in the Simulated Concrete Pore Solution.
papers.system: Q235 steel immersed in a simulated concrete pore solution
papers.approach: Passivation tests performed at different temperatures (20 °C, 40 °C, 60 °C) with monitoring via EIS and analysis of film thickness and composition to assess kinetics and film stability
papers.findings: The passivation process occurs in two stages—a rapid passivation phase within 24 hours and a stable phase thereafter. Higher temperatures accelerate film formation and promote the formation of more Fe3+ (e.g., Fe2O3) compounds, resulting in thicker and, in some cases, more protective passive films.
papers.mechanism: Temperature influences both the formation rate and the chemical composition of the passive film. Enhanced thermal energy speeds up oxidation processes, thereby shifting the oxide composition toward more protective phases. The integrity and nature of this film affect subsequent corrosion behavior.

papers.title: An electrochemical study of pH influences on corrosion and passivation for a Q235 carbon steel in HNO3–NaNO2, HAc–NaNO2
papers.system: Q235 carbon steel in acidic environments with varying pH, in the presence of nitrite ions
papers.approach: Electrochemical methods including potentiodynamic polarization and EIS were used to study the corrosion and passivation behavior under controlled pH conditions
papers.findings: The studies revealed that the corrosion current density decreases and passive film resistance increases under favorable pH conditions. A wider passivation window is obtained in certain acidic media indicating that electrolyte chemistry strongly influences the repassivation process.
papers.mechanism: The formation and stability of the passive film are sensitive not only to chloride attack but also to pH and the presence of specific ions (e.g., NO2–) that promote repassivation, thereby affecting the overall electrochemical protection.

established: Pre-exposed Q235 steel, when pickled and passivated, acquires a uniform, dense passivation film that provides an initial electrochemical barrier against corrosion.

Corrosion in Q235 steel progresses through distinct stages—from passivation film integrity to localized film rupture (often initiated by chloride ion attack), leading to pitting and subsequent rust formation.
Temperature and pH critically modulate the kinetics of passivation film formation and its chemical composition, which in turn influences the corrosion rate.

approaches_tried.approach: Cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion tests on pre-passivated Q235 steel
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified sequential stages in corrosion behavior, demonstrating that the initial passivation film delays corrosion but eventually suffers localized breakdown, leading to pitting and rapid degradation.

approaches_tried.approach: Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) and film analysis at various temperatures
approaches_tried.outcome: Showed that higher temperatures accelerate the formation and modify the properties of the passive film, suggesting thermal treatment could influence corrosion resistance.

approaches_tried.approach: Electrochemical studies in acidic environments with controlled pH and inhibitor species
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that environmental chemistry (pH, NO2– presence) plays a crucial role in determining passivation behavior and the overall corrosion rate.

mechanisms: The integrity and chemical composition of the pre-formed passivation film govern the initial protection of Q235 steel.
Chloride ions can infiltrate and locally disrupt the passivation film, leading to pitting corrosion and subsequent rust layer formation.
Temperature enhances oxidation kinetics, altering the passive film (e.g., increasing Fe2O3 content) and potentially shifting the balance between protective film formation and rupture.
disagreements: There is some divergence on whether higher temperatures invariably lead to improved passivation; in some cases, thermal energy may induce film defects or rupture, countering the expected benefits.

The exact role of environmental factors (pH, chloride concentration) can lead to competing mechanisms where enhanced repassivation may occur concurrently with film breakdown, making the net effect on corrosion rate variable.
open_questions: What is the critical threshold of passivation film integrity at which the transition from protection to accelerated corrosion occurs across different temperatures?
How do pre-existing microstructural inhomogeneities or defects in the passivation film influence its breakdown under variable salt and temperature conditions?
What is the interplay between annealing (or post-HEA treatments) and pre-formed passivation films in dictating long-term corrosion performance in Q235 steel?
opportunities: Design a controlled study that exposes pre-passivated Q235 steel to both room- and high-temperature regimes (700–900 °C) under identical salt exposure, monitoring electrochemical parameters and film integrity in real time.

Investigate composite or layered systems where a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating is applied and annealed atop Q235 steel to determine if modified passivation film dynamics can enhance corrosion resistance.

Combine temperature-gradient studies with localized surface analytical techniques (e.g., in situ SEM or EIS mapping) to correlate microstructural film breakdown with macroscopic corrosion rate changes, thereby isolating the governing causes.

directions.direction: Investigate the thermal‐induced chemical and mechanical evolution of the pre‐formed passivation film under aggressive salt exposure.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the question of why corrosion protection fails at high temperatures (700–900 °C) by examining film transformation, cracking, and chloride penetration. The physics of thermal oxidation and stress‐induced cracking are well established, and evidence from cyclic salt spray tests (e.g., PMC9504384) and high‐temperature EIS studies (PMC9867134) supports this line. It is experimentally feasible with high‐temperature corrosion cells and microanalysis.

directions.direction: Examine the effects of controlled annealing on the passivation film integrity to see if thermal pre-treatment can stabilize or further degrade corrosion protection.
directions.assessment: This study isolates the impact of a controlled annealing process on film defect density, drawing on reported differences in oxide phases at higher temperatures (PMC9867134). It directly interrogates whether residual stress relaxation can enhance protective film stability and is feasible using controlled furnaces and salt exposure tests.

directions.direction: Use in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) at varying temperatures to quantify changes in the passive film’s semiconductor properties and defect density.
directions.assessment: This direction uses well‐understood EIS methods to probe the barrier properties of the passive film under different temperature regimes. The approach is quantitatively supported by earlier EIS studies (PMC9867134) and offers a direct monitoring of charge transfer resistance changes, though technical challenges exist for high‐temperature in situ measurements.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of microstructural inhomogeneities (e.g., grain boundaries, minor defects) in initiating localized film breakdown via thermal cycling.
directions.assessment: This approach examines how inherent microstructural defects serve as preferential sites for passivation film rupture under thermal stresses and salt exposure. It addresses the localized breakdown mechanism emphasized in several studies (PMC9504384) and is experimentally accessible through controlled thermal cycling and microscopic analysis.

directions.direction: Combine high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating studies with subsequent annealing on Q235 steel to determine if advanced surface modifications alter passivation dynamics.
directions.assessment: While innovative, this direction shifts focus toward modified systems and layered architectures. Although related HEA studies exist, it diverts from the central question about the unmodified pre-exposure state of Q235 steel and would introduce additional variables. Thus, it is less direct relative to the constraints.

candidates.hypothesis: At high-temperature salt exposures (~800 °C), the pre-formed passivation film on Q235 steel transforms into a brittle, defect-rich Fe-oxide layer that readily cracks under thermal stresses, permitting aggressive chloride ion penetration and accelerating localized pitting corrosion.
candidates.intervention: Expose samples to cyclic salt spray in a controlled furnace at 800 °C versus a reference exposure at room temperature (25 °C).

candidates.hypothesis: A controlled annealing treatment of pre-passivated Q235 steel at 700 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere prior to salt exposure leads to partial relaxation of residual stress and defect reduction in the passive film, thereby enhancing its protective properties during subsequent high-temperature (700 °C) salt attack.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to a controlled thermal annealing treatment at 700 °C for 1 hour in an inert (argon) atmosphere followed by salt exposure at 700 °C.

candidates.hypothesis: Increasing the environmental temperature from room temperature to 800 °C in a chloride solution systematically decreases the charge transfer resistance (Rct) of the pre-formed passive film on Q235 steel due to increased defect density and altered semiconductor properties, thereby leading to higher corrosion current densities.
candidates.intervention: Expose samples to a series of controlled temperatures (25 °C, 400 °C, and 800 °C) in an identical aggressive NaCl environment while performing in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).

candidates.hypothesis: Under thermal cycling between room temperature and 800 °C in a chloride-rich environment, localized microstructural inhomogeneities such as grain boundaries in pre-passivated Q235 steel act as preferential sites for passive film rupture, initiating pitting corrosion that is significantly more pronounced than under isothermal conditions.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to thermal cycling (e.g., 5 minutes at 800 °C followed by 55 minutes at room temperature, repeated over several cycles) in an aggressive NaCl environment.
